nuggets.summary: Microsoft's old startup program, BizSpark, tried to win startups over by handing out cloud credits, essentially competing in a "credit war" with AWS and GCP. It backfired: startups had no loyalty to the credits themselves, so they'd burn through Microsoft's credits, move to AWS for its credits, then GCP, then circle back to Microsoft under a new company name to claim another round of free credits. The lesson for anyone building a startup-acquisition or partner program is that giving away a fungible resource (money-equivalent credits) buys usage, not loyalty, and creates a gaming incentive rather than a real relationship — the fix Microsoft landed on was to compete on distribution and revenue access instead of price.

Three years before this interview, Jorgensen struggled to get enterprise customers to take startup vendors seriously — big companies worried a small vendor might not exist in a few months and treated startup pitches with skepticism even when Microsoft made the introduction. By the time of this talk, the dynamic had inverted: enterprises were proactively asking Microsoft for more startup and disruptor solutions because they'd started treating outside innovation as a way to build new monetizable revenue streams and modernize IT rather than a risk to manage. The actionable read for founders: the "will you still be around" objection from enterprise buyers is not a fixed, permanent barrier — it can flip within a few years as a market's appetite for disruption catches up, so it's worth periodically re-testing an enterprise segment you wrote off before.

Jorgensen's concrete advice to founders pitching into a large partner channel (and to any startup pitching a broad market) is to abandon horizontal positioning — describing yourself as, say, "a security provider" — because a generic category doesn't tell a salesperson or customer what specific problem you solve or who to bring you to. Instead she tells founders to pick one vertical and go absurdly narrow inside it: her literal example is picking the Northwest region within healthcare and naming the top five target customers there, rather than claiming you can serve the whole industry everywhere. The non-obvious part is that narrowing scope this hard doesn't shrink opportunity in her experience — sellers can't act on an offer they can't categorize, so a startup that lets itself be put "in a box" actually gets moved faster than one that insists it can serve everyone.

Before Microsoft puts a startup's pitch in front of its 45,000 sellers, the team runs the pitch through a specific test: is it "Sesame Street simple" — simple enough that a salesperson who hears it for only two seconds immediately understands what the product does and can picture which of their own accounts it fits? They literally test draft pitches on sellers who already juggle many third-party offerings and watch for the ones who instantly say they get it and can see it applying to their own accounts, versus the ones who need it re-explained. The actionable takeaway is a cheap, concrete pitch-validation method: hand your one-liner to someone who is not a domain expert and has many other things competing for their attention, and treat their immediate, unprompted recognition (or confusion) as the real signal — not whether people who already understand your space nod along.

Jorgensen argues against the common startup instinct to compete on technology quality or on price, stating flatly that technology differentiation only lasts a limited window in any market (competitors normalize to feature parity within about 12 months) and that price differentiation never holds because anyone can drop their price. Her conclusion is that the only sustainable differentiator for Microsoft's own cloud business — and by extension for the startups it works with — is go-to-market: the ability to help a customer actually acquire distribution and revenue, not the underlying product or its cost. This runs counter to the default founder mental model that a better or cheaper product is the moat; the more durable strategy is investing in how the product gets distributed and sold.

Based on working with many startups, Jorgensen observes that most begin with a direct sales force built from their own engineers, and distribution channels — resellers, marketplaces, partner networks — are typically the very last thing founders think through, usually only once they're already under pressure to scale. This means most startups never explicitly design their business model around how they'll pay a channel, how they'll pay their own direct sales team, and how those two motions coexist, until it's an urgent problem rather than a planned one. The actionable fix she recommends is to treat channel/marketplace architecture as a first-class part of the business model from early on, not an afterthought bolted on once direct sales stalls.

Microsoft for Startups has an explicit, stated filter for who it will actually work with one-on-one: B2B/commercial-space companies, at Seed or Series A stage, generally with no more than $10 million in annual funding, and — critically — companies that already have a sellable product rather than something still in beta being tested for market viability. Anyone still validating product-market fit is routed to broader community events and technical resources instead of the individualized go-to-market support. This is a concrete, checkable bar: a startup evaluating whether Microsoft's program is worth pursuing can self-screen against whether it has a real, sellable-to-enterprise product yet before investing time in outreach.

When Microsoft's own executives debate strategy internally, they keep reaching for "where's our next Snapchat/Uber" as the aspirational target, and Jorgensen pushes back on that framing every time. Her point is that a splashy consumer brand people have heard of is actually a bad target for a B2B-oriented program: consumer startups tend not to be loyal to any single cloud platform, and Microsoft has little compelling go-to-market value to offer them in return. She contrasts this with an unglamorous B2B disruptor (she names a Seattle healthcare startup, Kensai, that almost nobody outside its own industry has heard of) that could become the dominant player in its vertical and be extremely valuable to Microsoft's enterprise customers without ever being a household name — the reframe being that being consumer-famous and being commercially important are different axes, and chasing the former is often a distraction from the latter.

For a founder trying to actually get inside Microsoft's startup program, Jorgensen gives a specific, practical routing tip: don't rely on informal networking or trying to reach her or a specific contact directly — email startups@microsoft.com (spelled out: "startups," plural, no hyphen, at microsoft.com), which she says gets faster attention than going through personal connections. That inbox is the front door that triages what the founder needs (go-to-market help, technical architecture guidance, etc.) and routes accordingly, including flagging early that Microsoft's benefit structure works like a loyalty/rewards program — the more a company builds on Azure or Dynamics, the more support and benefits unlock.
